newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam delays banking revamp as crisis looms.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam delays banking revamp as crisis looms.

text.p: Vietnam said on Thursday it had delayed a scheduled revamp of banking laws to allow time to fix existing problems in an industry whose woes one official said evoked the failed savings schemes that brought chaos to Albania.

The National Assembly office said draft legislation concerning the central bank and credit institutions had been scratched from the agenda of the legislative body's spring session, which starts next Wednesday.
"We came to the conclusion that the quality of those two draft laws do not meet the requirements," the assembly's office director, Vu Mao, told a news conference.
The two drafts were aimed at liberalising the industry and tightening prudential and supervisory regulations.
Mao said revised drafts would go before the legislature in September and that in the meantime, the banking sector would have to deal with its problems under existing law.
However, he said existing ordinances put in place during the early years of the communist government's decade-old experiment in market reforms were now outdated.

"Therefore, they have some shortcomings and...there are some problems in the banking sector which need to be dealt with," he said, adding a reference to the savings schemes in Albania that bankrupted thousands and led to anarchy throughout the country.
Mao's unusually frank comments came at a time of growing concern over the health of Vietnam's fledgling banking sector.

Industry sources say many banks, both state-owned and privately held, are saddled with huge debt due to years of politically inspired lending, exposure to the now-slumping real estate market and a spree of credit guarantees for imports in 1996.
The debt problem came under the spotlight last month after reports that a highly respected private bank had failed to meet the payment deadline on a letter of credit.
Nerves were jangled again this week when two prominent business executives were arrested in Ho Chi Minh City for their alleged involvement in a massive bank loans scam.

Fearing for the reputation of its financial system as rumours swirled, the government this week listed various areas related to the banking sector that were barred or restricted from media coverage under state secrecy laws.
Mao said that although there were big problems in the banking system, it was unwise to exaggerate them.
He said the government had always managed to settle its difficulties in the past and noted the central bank would emerge from the new legislation with a stronger supervisory hand.
He refused to be drawn out on whether banks would be allowed to fold, but noted that banks were corporations and, as such, were governed by Vietnam's bankruptcy law just like all other corporations.
Vietnam created four big state-run banks out of the central bank in 1990. A host of smaller privately held banks -- known as joint-stock banks -- sprang up after that.

Efforts are already under way to tighten supervision of the scandal-ridden banking system and bring its primitive accounting practices closer to international standards. Among the issues needed to be cleared up is the industry's failure to recognise the Western concept of bad or non-performing debt.
